title: Partial regularity for Double Phase obstacle problems: the Euler-Lagrange system for constrained local minimizers (printed as Theorem 3.1)
author: Filomena De Filippis, Antonella Nastasi, Cintia Pacchiano Camacho
work: Partial regularity for Double Phase obstacle problems
difficulty_reason: Counted unit: the article's Theorem 3.1 (source0.tex lines 788--797), the Euler-Lagrange system satisfied by a constrained local minimizer of the double phase functional with target as in condition (a), delivered with the article's complete original proof at source0.tex lines 798--847 (50 lines, one adjacent proof environment, no gap and no deferral). The proof is not a routine verification: for a general target set the minimisation property cannot be linearised by a convexity argument, and the article says so explicitly. The author argument covers the boundary of the target with finitely many balls, builds a partition of unity and a local frame of vector fields tangent to the boundary, decomposes an arbitrary test field into its tangential and normal parts, and then varies the minimiser in two different ways: along the flow of a tangential field, which produces the identity that becomes the left-hand side of the system, and along the normal field v, which produces a Radon measure lambda through the Riesz representation theorem and then, after proving that lambda does not depend on the cut-off parameter, a density function theta through the Radon-Nikodym theorem. Both variations are combined with the partition of unity and the identity d/ddelta of the functional at delta = 0 to yield the stated system. The substantive steps are the construction of the test fields, the identification of the limit of the two boundary integrals as the cut-off parameter vanishes using the tangential identity for the distance function, and the passage from the Radon measure to its boundary density; none of them is an unpacking of definitions. H2: a complete original research-paper theorem, moderately short, whose proof is a genuinely technical variational argument rather than a routine exercise.
